title: Riesz Potentials and the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev Inequality

items.title: Riesz potential of order alpha
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice for the Euclidean Lebesgue framework. For n>=1 and 0<alpha<n fix the unit normalization c_{n,alpha}=1 and K_alpha(z)=|z|^{alpha-n} for z!=0 (the value at zero is immaterial). For a measurable complex f define I_alpha f(x)=c_{n,alpha} integral_{R^n} K_alpha(x-y)f(y)dy precisely at points x where the integral of K_alpha(x-y)|f(y)| is finite. This definition alone makes no all-Lp existence assertion.
items.strategy: Fix c_{n,alpha}=1, matching Williams Proposition 11.4 and Harboure §1. The kernel is positive off its null singular point, and the integral is first a pointwise absolutely convergent Lebesgue integral. The next lemma proves local kernel integrability, Lp almost-everywhere existence in the strict range, and representative independence; no Fourier-symbol identity is asserted.

references.title: Mark Williams, Notes on Harmonic Analysis, §11.2, Proposition 11.4, printed p. 73
Eleonor Harboure, Spaces of Smooth Functions, §1, printed p. 1

items.title: Near and far bounds for a Riesz potential
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let n>=1, 0<alpha<n, 1<p<n/alpha and f in complex Lp(R^n). Every measurable representative is locally integrable. At every x with Mf(x)<infinity, and for every R>0, the absolute near and far integrals N_R(x)=integral_{|x-y|<R}|x-y|^{alpha-n}|f(y)|dy and F_R(x)=integral_{|x-y|>=R}|x-y|^{alpha-n}|f(y)|dy are finite and satisfy N_R(x)<=C_{n,alpha}R^alpha Mf(x) and F_R(x)<=C_{n,alpha,p}R^{alpha-n/p}||f||p. The far bound holds at every x. Each convergent integral is representative-independent; where both converge, so is the total potential.
items.proof_strategy: Use complex Hölder on each finite-measure ball to show Lp is locally L1, so the published centered Mf applies. Set v_n=|B(0,1)|>0; the C1 change-of-variables theorem applied to dilation gives |B(x,r)|=v_n r^n. On shells 2^{-j-1}R<=|x-y|<2^{-j}R, the negative kernel power is at most (2^{-j-1}R)^{alpha-n}, while the ball integral is at most v_n(2^{-j}R)^n Mf(x); sum the geometric series in 2^{-j alpha}. For the far region apply Hölder to |f| and the Borel kernel, translate to the origin by change of variables and use the published polar formula: integral_R^infinity r^{(alpha-n)p'+n-1}dr is finite exactly when (n-alpha)p'>n, equivalently p<n/alpha, and its 1/p' power is a constant times R^{alpha-n/p}. If representatives differ on a null set, the nonnegative kernel integrals agree, hence so do convergent complex integrals. No estimate is asserted at a point with infinite Mf.

references.title: Mark Williams, Notes on Harmonic Analysis, Proposition 11.4, printed p. 73
Larry Guth, Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev Inequality, §3, printed p. 3

items.title: Hedberg pointwise inequality for Riesz potentials
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For n>=1, 0<alpha<n, 1<p<n/alpha, theta=alpha p/n in (0,1), f in complex Lp(R^n), and every x with Mf(x)<infinity, the integral I_alpha f(x) converges absolutely and |I_alpha f(x)|<=C_{n,alpha,p}(Mf(x))^{1-theta}||f||p^theta. If ||f||p=0 or Mf(x)=0, the potential is zero at the stated point, so no undefined zero/infinity power is used.
items.proof_strategy: The near/far lemma gives |I_alpha f(x)|<=C(R^alpha M+R^{alpha-n/p}F), with M=Mf(x), F=||f||p. If F=0, complex Lp norm definiteness gives f=0 a.e. and hence I=0. If M=0 and F>0, let R tend to infinity; the negative exponent alpha-n/p makes the far term vanish while the near term stays zero. If 0<M,F<infinity, select R=(F/M)^{p/n}; then R^alpha M=M^{1-alpha p/n}F^{alpha p/n}=R^{alpha-n/p}F. This is the claimed bound, with no optimization at an infinite maximal value.

references.title: Mark Williams, Notes on Harmonic Analysis, Proposition 11.4, printed p. 73
Larry Guth, Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev Inequality, §3, printed p. 3

items.title: Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev fractional integration inequality
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let n>=1, 0<alpha<n and 1<p<n/alpha, and set 1/q=1/p-alpha/n. Then q is finite and greater than p. The unit-normalized Riesz integral I_alpha f exists absolutely for almost every x for every f in complex Lp(R^n), defines a representative-independent bounded linear map I_alpha:Lp(R^n;C)->Lq(R^n;C), and satisfies ||I_alpha f||q<=C_{n,alpha,p}||f||p. On C_c^infinity the map is the pointwise integral; its unique bounded dense-core extension is the same almost-everywhere integral operator.
items.proof_strategy: Put theta=alpha p/n, so q=p/(1-theta), q(1-theta)=p, and q>p. Apply the published centered maximal Lp theorem to the nonnegative real modulus |f|; this makes Mf finite a.e. The near/far and Hedberg lemmas then give absolute integral existence and |I_alpha f|^q<=C(Mf)^p||f||p^{qtheta}. Integration and ||Mf||p<=C||f||p yield the stated norm bound, first for the smooth core. For arbitrary Lebesgue-measurable f, set the kernel value at zero to zero: (x,y)->K_alpha(x-y) is Borel on the Euclidean product, and (x,y)->f(y) is measurable for the Lebesgue product sigma-algebra because it is a coordinate projection. Their product is thus product-measurable without precomposing f with a noninjective map. Euclidean Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite, so Tonelli on the positive and negative parts of its real and imaginary components makes x->I_alpha f(x) measurable on the full-measure absolute-convergence set. The near/far lemma makes its Lq class representative-independent; absolute integrals make it linear. The same pointwise bound proves boundedness for all f. Since complex smooth compact support is dense and complex Lq is complete, the published bounded-dense-subspace extension theorem applies after the core norm bound; uniqueness identifies that extension with this integral-defined bounded map. Countable Choice is spent by the maximal, measure, density, completeness, and extension interfaces; full AC is not used.

references.title: Mark Williams, Notes on Harmonic Analysis, Proposition 11.4, printed p. 73
Larry Guth, Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev Inequality, Theorem 0.2 and §3, printed pp. 1, 3
Eleonor Harboure, Spaces of Smooth Functions, Theorem 1, printed pp. 2–5

items.title: Endpoint bounds require separate formulations
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice for the stated Lebesgue conventions. Recorded orientation, not proved here: for 0<alpha<n, the Riesz potential has a weak L1-to-L^{n/(n-alpha),infinity} bound; the strong HLS theorem does not include p=1. At p=n/alpha, a compactly supported input has a BMO mean-oscillation bound, while for general L^{n/alpha} data the critical potential must be renormalized modulo constants before the BMO statement is made. None of these endpoint claims is a proof supplier for this pair.
items.strategy: Harboure §1 Theorem 3 gives the weak lower endpoint and explicitly denies its strong counterpart; Theorem 4 gives the BMO seminorm estimate only for compactly supported critical input, and the following remark subtracts the far kernel to define a general critical class modulo constants. State these as recorded boundary facts with their exact hypotheses. The local Hedberg route requires strong Lp boundedness of Mf and strict far-region Hölder integrability, so it proves neither endpoint.

references.title: Eleonor Harboure, Spaces of Smooth Functions, §1 Theorems 3–4 and following remark, printed pp. 5–7

external_dependency.exact_statement: For 0<alpha<n, I_alpha maps L1 to weak L^{n/(n-alpha)}; for compactly supported f in L^{n/alpha}, I_alpha f has BMO seminorm at most C||f||_{n/alpha}; the general critical class uses a far-kernel subtraction modulo constants.
external_dependency.local_proof_attempt: The local near/far argument lacks a strong L1 maximal bound at p=1, and its far-region Holder integral is logarithmically divergent at p=n/alpha. The separate weak and BMO proofs in Harboure §1 are recorded but are not reconstructed or consumed here.
external_dependency.necessity: Documents the exact boundary of the strong theorem and prevents either endpoint from being substituted into the Stein–Tomas supplier.

title: Riesz Potentials and the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev Inequality: Examples

items.title: Dilation determines the Riesz-potential target exponent
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Fix n>=1 and 0<alpha<n. If a uniform estimate ||I_alpha f||q<=C||f||p holds for every complex C_c^infinity(R^n) function with 1<=p,q<infinity, then necessarily 1/q=1/p-alpha/n. For f_lambda(x)=f(lambda x), the two norms scale by lambda^{-n/p} and lambda^{-alpha-n/q}, respectively; a nonzero nonnegative test function makes the comparison nontrivial.
items.proof_strategy: Use the published smooth bump between concentric balls to choose a nonzero nonnegative f in C_c^infinity. Its potential is positive on an open set, so a supposed finite-norm bound gives 0<||I_alpha f||q<infinity. For lambda>0 set f_lambda(x)=f(lambda x). Change variables z=lambda y in the integral to obtain I_alpha f_lambda(x)=lambda^{-alpha}(I_alpha f)(lambda x); the published C1 change-of-variables formula gives ||f_lambda||p=lambda^{-n/p}||f||p and ||I_alpha f_lambda||q=lambda^{-alpha-n/q}||I_alpha f||q. Apply the same bound to every lambda; sending lambda to zero and infinity forces alpha+n/q=n/p. The strict HLS theorem is not used as a premise of this necessity argument.

references.title: Eleonor Harboure, Spaces of Smooth Functions, remark following Theorem 1, printed p. 2
Larry Guth, Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev Inequality, Proposition 0.1, printed p. 1

items.title: Strong fractional integration fails at p equal to one
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let n>=1, 0<alpha<n and q0=n/(n-alpha). For every epsilon>0 the normalized ball function f_epsilon=1_{B(0,epsilon)}/|B(0,epsilon)| has L1 norm one and is an approximate point mass. Its Riesz potential satisfies I_alpha f_epsilon(x)>=C_{n,alpha}|x|^{alpha-n} for |x|>2epsilon, so I_alpha f_epsilon is not in L^{q0}(R^n). Thus no strong L1-to-L^{q0} version of the HLS estimate holds.
items.proof_strategy: The published ball lemma gives 0<|B(0,epsilon)|<infinity, hence ||f_epsilon||1=1. For each continuous compactly supported test phi, the difference between its f_epsilon-average and phi(0) is at most sup_{|y|<epsilon}|phi(y)-phi(0)|, tending to zero; this proves the approximate-point-mass phrase. For |x|>2epsilon and y in the ball, |x-y|<=|x|+epsilon<3|x|/2. Since alpha-n<0, |x-y|^{alpha-n}>=(3|x|/2)^{alpha-n}; integrate against the probability density f_epsilon. Raise to q0=n/(n-alpha), so q0(alpha-n)=-n. The published polar formula gives integral_{|x|>2epsilon}|x|^{-n}dx=sigma(S^{n-1}) integral_{2epsilon}^infinity dr/r=infinity. This direct fixed-epsilon tail proves failure of the strong endpoint; the approximate-point-mass limit is explanatory, not a hidden Fatou step.

references.title: Eleonor Harboure, Spaces of Smooth Functions, Theorem 3 and following remark, printed p. 5
Larry Guth, Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev Inequality, Proposition 0.1, printed p. 1

items.title: The critical Riesz potential can diverge and be essentially unbounded
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let n>=1, 0<alpha<n and p0=n/alpha>1. Define f(0)=0 and f(y)=|y|^{-alpha}/log(e/|y|) for 0<|y|<e^{-1}, with f(y)=0 outside that punctured ball. Then f belongs to L^{p0}(R^n), but I_alpha f(0)=+infinity and I_alpha f is essentially unbounded near zero. Thus the raw potential is not a bounded L^{p0}-to-L-infinity map.
items.proof_strategy: Use polar integration to compute ||f||_{p0}^{p0}=sigma(S^{n-1}) integral_0^{e^{-1}} dr/[r(log(e/r))^{p0}], finite because p0>1. At x=0 the absolute potential is sigma(S^{n-1}) integral_0^{e^{-1}} dr/[r log(e/r)], which diverges. For 0<|x|<e^{-1}/2, integrate only over 2|x|<|y|<e^{-1}; there |x-y|<=3|y|/2, so the negative kernel power gives I_alpha f(x)>=C integral_{2|x|}^{e^{-1}} dr/[r log(e/r)]. This tends to infinity as |x| approaches zero, hence every arbitrarily high superlevel set contains a punctured ball of positive measure. Divergence at one point alone is not used to infer failure of an essential-supremum bound.

references.title: Eleonor Harboure, Spaces of Smooth Functions, critical-p radial example, printed p. 5
